steps.body:
∫ 2x dx = x² + C is a **family**: a stack of identical parabolas, one for every C.

They all have the same slope at every x — which is exactly why the derivative could not tell them apart. To choose one, you need a single extra fact: **one point the curve passes through.**

That fact is called an *initial condition*, and it pins C.

explanationVariants: F(x) = x² + C, and F(1) = 5 gives 1 + C = 5, so C = 4. Then F(x) = x² + 4 and F(3) = 13.
The derivative told you the SHAPE; the initial condition told you the HEIGHT.

numericErrors.feedback: That is 3² — you took C = 0. But F(1) = 5 forces 1 + C = 5, so C = 4 and F(3) = 9 + 4 = 13.
That is F(1), the given value. F(3) = 3² + 4 = 13.
Check C: F(1) = 1 + C = 5 gives C = 4, not 5. So F(3) = 9 + 4 = 13.

widget.prompt: Why one point is exactly enough.

panels.title: The family
panels.body: x², x² + 1, x² + 7, x² − 3 — an infinite stack of parabolas, each one a vertical shift of the last. Every one of them has derivative 2x.

panels.title: Why the derivative cannot choose
panels.body: Sliding a curve UP does not tilt it anywhere. So the slope function carries no information at all about the vertical position — the information was destroyed, not hidden.

panels.title: One point restores it
panels.body: Say the curve passes through (1, 5). Exactly one member of the stack does that. The initial condition does not add new calculus; it replaces the information the derivative threw away.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third panel says what an initial condition actually IS.
widget.successFeedback: The derivative destroys vertical position. A single point puts it back, and picks one curve out of infinitely many.

steps.body: The reveal made a claim about the whole family at once. Now hold the family in your hands: slide the curve and watch the derivative refuse to react.

predict.prompt: The top pane shows f(x) = x², the bottom traces f′. If you slide the WHOLE curve upward, what happens in the f′ pane?

options.label: f′ rises too — the curve went up
Nothing at all — f′ does not move
f′ tilts, because the curve is steeper up there

predict.reveal: Nothing moves. Sliding a curve up does not tilt it anywhere, so every member of the family x² + C has the identical derivative 2x. That is why the derivative alone can never tell you which member you have — and why an initial condition is not extra calculus, it is the missing information put back.

widget.prompt: Slide C until the curve passes through the point (1, 5), then bring x to 1. Watch the f′ pane the whole time.
widget.successFeedback: At x = 1 the tangent's slope is 2 — and it was 2 for every single value of C you slid through, because a vertical shift tilts nothing. The point (1, 5) is what picked C = 4 out of the infinite stack: 1 + C = 5. The derivative gave you the shape; one point gave you the position.
widget.lowFeedback: You are left of x = 1. Keep going — and notice that whatever you do with the C slider on the way, the f′ trace underneath is unchanged.
widget.highFeedback: You have gone past x = 1. Come back — and watch the f′ pane as you slide C: it does not care where the curve sits vertically, which is the whole reason C survives differentiation unseen.

explanationVariants: v(t) = 2t means s(t) = t² + C, and s(0) = 10 gives C = 10. So s(3) = 9 + 10 = 19.
The velocity tells you how the position CHANGES; the starting position tells you where it changes FROM.

widget.prompt: A particle has velocity v(t) = 2t and starts at position s(0) = 10. Find s(3).

numericErrors.feedback: That is the DISTANCE travelled, ∫₀³ 2t dt = 9. It must be added to the starting position of 10.
That is where it started. In 3 seconds it also travelled 9, so it ends at 19.
That is v(3), the velocity at the final instant — not a position at all.

steps.body:
That is the shape of every problem in the next course:

**A rate + a starting value = the whole story.**

The rate gives the shape (the antiderivative). The starting value gives the height (the constant). Neither one alone is enough, and together they are always enough.

explanationVariants: Knowing only the rate leaves C unknown, so the position is known only up to a constant — you know how far it moved, not where it is.
The tank problem is the same: a flow rate tells you how much ARRIVED, never how much was there to begin with.

widget.prompt: You know a tank's inflow rate for the whole day but not how full it started. What can you find?

options.label: How much water was ADDED — but not how much is in the tank.
options.feedback: Right. The integral of a rate gives the CHANGE. The starting amount is the constant, and no rate can tell you what it was.

options.label: Exactly how much is in the tank.
options.feedback: Not without the starting level. Two tanks with identical inflows can hold wildly different amounts.

options.label: Nothing useful.
options.feedback: You get the total change, which is often exactly what is wanted — just not the absolute level.

options.label: The final level, if you assume it started empty.
options.feedback: That is an assumption, and it is precisely the extra fact — the initial condition — that the problem did not give you.

hints: Acceleration integrates to velocity, and velocity integrates to position — so you will integrate TWICE and meet TWO constants.
a(t) = 6t → v(t) = 3t² + C₁, and v(0) = 2 gives C₁ = 2.
v(t) = 3t² + 2 → s(t) = t³ + 2t + C₂, and s(0) = 1 gives C₂ = 1. Now find s(2).
explanationVariants: Each integration introduces one constant, and each initial condition kills one. Two of each, and the answer is pinned exactly.

numericErrors.feedback: That is 8 + 4 — you dropped the second constant. s(0) = 1 gives C₂ = 1, so s(2) = 13.
That is t³ alone. The velocity's constant of 2 contributes a 2t term, worth 4 at t = 2, and then s(0) = 1 adds one more.
Check C₁: v(0) = 2 gives C₁ = 2, not 3. Then s(2) = 8 + 4 + 1 = 13.

steps.body: A rate plus a starting value is the whole story.
takeaways: ∫ f dx is a FAMILY of curves; an initial condition picks one out of it.
The derivative destroys vertical position, so no amount of calculus can recover it — only a given point can.
Integrate twice and you meet two constants, which need two conditions to pin down.
steps.teaser: Next: the antiderivatives of the rest of the function library.

concept.body: Three steps. **Integrate**, keeping the + C. **Substitute** the given point. **Solve** for C. Only then answer the question that was actually asked.

explanationVariants: F(x) = x² + C with F(2) = 10 gives 4 + C = 10, so C = 6.

commonErrors.feedback: That is F(2), the value given. Substitute it: 4 + C = 10, so C = 6.
That is 2² — the x² part. The constant is what is LEFT: 10 − 4 = 6.
